title: Earnings and Event Risk
summary: Record revenue can accompany a falling stock. What matters is the change in expectations for future profit and cash.
body_markdown:
A company can report record revenue and see its stock fall. The apparent contradiction disappears once you separate three questions: did the business grow, did it beat what investors expected, and did the report improve the value of future cash flows?


An earnings trade is usually about the second and third questions. The headline alone answers neither very well.


## What the market expected


Start with the variables that drive the business. For a retailer, sales growth, gross margin and inventory can matter together. For a subscription business, customer retention and the cost of acquiring growth may explain more than revenue alone.


Write down what would count as a meaningful surprise and where that expectation came from: management guidance, published analyst estimates or your own model. They are different benchmarks. A company can beat consensus while disappointing investors who had quietly expected more.


The[SEC’s guide to reading a 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/files/reada10k.pdf) explains where to find the business description, risk factors, financial statements and management’s discussion. Use those materials to understand the machine producing the numbers before deciding which single number deserves attention.


## Revenue, profit, and cash


Suppose the market expects revenue of $100 million and an operating margin of 20%, implying $20 million of operating profit. Actual revenue is $110 million, but margin is 16%. Operating profit is $17.6 million: revenue beats by 10%, while profit falls 12% short of that expectation.


**$110 million × 16% = $17.6 million.**


The next question is why. A temporary launch expense has different implications from permanent price cuts needed to retain customers. Strong sales funded by unusually generous customer credit may also look better in revenue than in collected cash.


Earnings per share adds another layer because the share count matters. Total profit of $100 million divided by 100 million shares gives $1 per share. The same profit divided by 90 million shares gives about $1.11. That can be a genuine benefit to remaining shareholders, but it is different from an 11% improvement in the operating business.


When a release emphasizes adjusted earnings, read the reconciliation. Ask whether excluded costs are unusual in substance or recur as part of running the company. Apply that judgment consistently to both favorable and unfavorable quarters.


## The quarter and the outlook


A completed quarter describes what has happened. Guidance, orders, pricing and capital spending help form a view of what comes next. A strong quarter followed by weaker guidance can rationally produce a lower price.


Trace each development through both sides of the income statement. Higher investment spending can improve a supplier’s revenue while reducing the buyer’s near-term free cash flow. Calling the same announcement “bullish for the sector” skips the question of who receives the money and who must fund it.


Price also matters. A business improvement already embedded in a demanding valuation may offer less new information than a modest improvement nobody expected. You are comparing the update with a price, not grading the company’s management presentation.


## Holding through the announcement


An ordinary-session stop does not ensure an ordinary-session loss around an announcement. A $4,000 position exposed to an 8% adverse gap loses roughly $320 before execution and financing costs, even if a resting exit was intended to act much sooner.


The[SEC’s extended-hours bulletin](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/general-resources/news-alerts/alerts-bulletins/investor-bulletins-42) describes thinner trading, wider spreads and prices that can differ from the next regular session. Those issues matter when a report arrives outside the underlying market’s main hours, including when a related perp continues to trade.


Separate the decision to hold through the release from the decision to trade after reading it. The first accepts uncertainty about the information itself. The second accepts that some repricing has already occurred. Either requires a specific argument about what remains misunderstood, a feasible execution and a loss the account can bear.
